summary:
Mitochondria is an innovative web-based health monitoring console developed to support astronauts during space missions by transforming complex medical data into clear, actionable health insights.

Our solution focuses on four critical areas: Bone Health, Cardiovascular Health, Immune Health, and Behavioral Health. Unlike conventional monitoring tools, Mitochondria combines predefined biological reasoning and scientific relationships between biomarkers with artificial intelligence to identify potential health risks, prioritize findings, visualize health trends, and generate comprehensive reports with personalized recommendations.

Astronauts can upload medical examinations or manually enter their results, while compatible Bluetooth devices enable real-time monitoring of physiological and environmental parameters.

The console also features three interconnected user roles: Astronaut, Researcher, and Medical. Newly detected biomarkers undergo scientific evaluation and medical approval before being integrated into the system, allowing its biomarker catalog to expand under human supervision.

By combining biological knowledge, AI-assisted analysis, real-time monitoring, and medical oversight, and drawing on scientific data and resources from NASA and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), Mitochondria addresses NASA's challenge of monitoring astronaut health, supporting earlier risk identification and better-informed decisions during long-duration space missions.

THE MITOCHONDRIA — PROJECT DETAILS

1. Project Overview

THE MITOCHONDRIA is a web-based astronaut health monitoring console developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our project aims to transform complex medical examinations and physiological measurements into integrated, understandable, and scientifically informed health reports.

Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to several health challenges, including bone loss, cardiovascular changes, immune dysregulation, sleep disturbances, and psychological stress. These effects can occur simultaneously and may influence one another.

Our console addresses these challenges by organizing health information into four interconnected domains:

  • Bone Health: Bone metabolism, mineral regulation, bone density, and musculoskeletal health.
  • Cardiovascular Health: Heart function, circulation, cardiovascular adaptation, and related biomarkers.
  • Immune Health: Immune function, inflammation, and infection-related indicators.
  • Behavioral Health: Sleep, recovery, psychological well-being, and cognitive performance.

Unlike approaches that consider every biomarker independently, THE MITOCHONDRIA combines structured biological reasoning and scientific evidence with AI-assisted analysis when appropriate.

The objective is to help astronauts and authorized medical personnel recognize potentially concerning findings, understand relevant biological relationships, monitor changes over time, and make better-informed decisions.

The console supports three principal health-related roles: Astronaut, Researcher, and Ground Medical. A separate Mission Operator role supports mission and crew administration.

THE MITOCHONDRIA is currently an open-source research prototype demonstrated using synthetic medical data. It is not clinically validated and does not replace medical professionals.

2. Astronaut Workflow — Uploading Medical Examinations

One of our main development priorities was to make medical data entry as straightforward as possible.

Astronauts can manually enter measurements or upload supported examination files, review the extracted information, and associate accepted observations with their authorized mission records.

Step 1 — Sign In as an Astronaut

Open the THE MITOCHONDRIA web console:

https://mitochondria.edocinfo.com/

From the homepage:

  1. Select Astronaut.
  2. Click Sign In.
  3. Access the astronaut workspace.

For the demonstration, prepared credentials simplify access to the synthetic environment.

Step 2 — Open Unified Data Intake

After signing in:

  1. Navigate to Unified Data Intake.
  2. Locate the field Authorized Mission & Crew.
  3. Open the dropdown menu.
  4. Select the following exact option:

MITOCHONDRIA 2026 – Synthetic Demonstration — Alex Morgan — Synthetic Astronaut

This option represents the authorized synthetic demonstration mission and crew member.

The interface may display the shorter selected label:

MITOCHONDRIA 2026 – Synthetic Demonstration — Alex Morgan

Another mission, FV01 Security Test B — FV01 Test Crew B, may also appear in the dropdown. This is not the mission used for our Alex Morgan demonstration.

Step 3 — Select Data Provenance

Next, locate the field:

Data Provenance (required)

For the demonstration, select the appropriate synthetic demonstration data option.

This identifies the information as fictional testing data rather than a genuine astronaut medical record.

Step 4 — Choose the Data Entry Method

THE MITOCHONDRIA provides two principal methods for entering medical information.

Option A — Manual Entry

The astronaut enters individual biological measurements, including the biomarker name, numerical value, measurement unit, and examination date.

Option B — File Upload

The astronaut uploads a supported examination file, such as PDF, CSV, or Excel.

The document-processing workflow assists with extracting and organizing biomarker names, measurement values, units, and dates.

The astronaut can then review the information before registration.

This reduces manual data entry while maintaining user oversight of the extracted observations.

Step 5 — Required Information for Our Synthetic Demonstration

Our prepared NASA Space Apps demonstration uses a predefined synthetic astronaut profile.

To associate an uploaded examination correctly with this demonstration profile, the file must contain the appropriate identifying information and examination data.

The following details are required for our prepared Alex Morgan demo:

  • Subject: Alex Morgan
  • Record: ALEX-MORGAN-SYN-001
  • Mission: MITO_DEMO_2026
  • Examination Date: A date not already used for the corresponding demo examination
  • Measurement: Biomarker name
  • Value: Numerical result
  • Unit: Measurement unit
  • Examination Date for Each Measurement: Date associated with each measurement

Important distinction: The mission identifier written inside the examination file is MITO_DEMO_2026. The mission option selected within Unified Data Intake is MITOCHONDRIA 2026 – Synthetic Demonstration — Alex Morgan — Synthetic Astronaut.

These two labels serve different purposes and should not be confused.

Example of a Synthetic Laboratory Examination

MITOCHONDRIA | Synthetic Laboratory Examinations

Subject: Alex Morgan
Record: ALEX-MORGAN-SYN-001
Mission: MITO_DEMO_2026
Examination date: 2026-11-11

SYNTHETIC DEMONSTRATION DATA — NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

Measurement

Value

Unit

Examination Date

Sodium

131

mmol/L

2026-11-11

A complete examination can contain multiple measurements following this structure.

The demonstration environment is specifically prepared for Alex Morgan. If the uploaded document contains a different subject identity or incompatible identifying information, the system may flag the discrepancy rather than automatically associating the results with Alex Morgan.

The examination date must also be checked against existing demonstration records to avoid duplicate submissions.

The date 2026-11-11 is an example of the required format, not a guarantee that this date remains available. Judges should choose a date that has not already been used for the corresponding examination in the demonstration record.

These restrictions apply to the prepared synthetic demonstration. They do not mean the broader console architecture is limited to a single astronaut.

Step 6 — Review the Extracted Results

After uploading the examination, the astronaut opens the review section.

Select:

Review All

The console presents the extracted observations, allowing the astronaut to inspect:

  • Biomarker names.
  • Recorded values.
  • Measurement units.
  • Examination dates.
  • Recognition and review status.

Recognized observations can proceed through the normal confirmation process.

Unknown or unresolved biomarkers may require a separate scientific review workflow.

Step 7 — Confirm the Examination

After reviewing the consolidated results, the astronaut confirms the accepted observations.

The accepted data are then associated with the authorized astronaut mission record.

These observations can subsequently support reports, longitudinal comparisons, and scientific interpretation.

3. Astronaut Health Report — Generating and Understanding the Results

After recording medical examinations, the astronaut can generate a comprehensive Health Intelligence Report.

Step 1 — Open Astronaut Health Report

Navigate to:

Astronaut Health Report

Step 2 — Select the Mission

Choose the appropriate authorized mission associated with the synthetic astronaut Alex Morgan.

Step 3 — Select the Examination Period

Choose the date range to be analyzed.

For example, selecting November 1–10, 2026 allows the console to examine available observations within that period.

If records exist on six dates, the report can identify those six actual examination dates rather than assuming that examinations were performed every day.

This allows the astronaut to compare observations collected at different points in time.

Step 4 — Generate the Report

In the prepared synthetic demonstration, the report workflow includes the option:

Load Authorized Synthetic Fixture

This loads the authorized synthetic demonstration data for the report.

The broader reporting architecture also includes server-confirmed mission data and an offline reporting path. The newer server-confirmed reporting workflow has been verified in the development Preview environment; it should not be represented as already published on the public website unless deployment has been confirmed.

Step 5 — High-Priority Findings

The Health Intelligence Report begins by highlighting potentially important findings.

These may include unusual biomarker values or combinations of measurements that deserve further attention.

For example, certain combinations of temperature and inflammatory indicators may suggest possible fever or inflammation.

The system prioritizes findings according to its available observations and scientific interpretation rules.

These findings are not medical diagnoses. They are intended to highlight areas that may require further investigation or professional evaluation.

Step 6 — Health Overview and Biological Reasoning

The report provides a broader overview of the astronaut's health.

A central objective of THE MITOCHONDRIA is to examine relevant scientific relationships between measurements from different physiological systems.

Rather than presenting every biomarker as an isolated result, the console organizes available information into a more integrated biological picture.

For example, scientific reasoning may consider relationships involving:

  • Bone metabolism and mineral regulation.
  • Cardiovascular adaptation and related physiological indicators.
  • Inflammation and immune activity.
  • Sleep, recovery, and physiological stress.

Scientific relationships are interpreted according to their available evidence and limitations.

The project distinguishes established evidence, exploratory relationships, and hypotheses. It does not treat every observed association as a proven causal relationship.

Artificial intelligence may assist with explanations or research questions, but AI-generated research content requires appropriate human scientific review.

Step 7 — Charts and Trend Review

The report includes visualizations to make complex medical information easier to understand.

These allow the astronaut to review the recorded measurements and examine changes over time.

The Trend Review section highlights longitudinal changes in biomarkers across available examination dates.

Charts can help users observe increasing, decreasing, or stable measurements.

Color-coded findings also make it easier to identify parameters requiring attention.

Step 8 — Personalized Recommendations

The report may present recommendations associated with the available measurements and identified findings.

Depending on the results, these may involve:

  • Nutrition and dietary considerations.
  • Physical activity and recovery.
  • Sleep and rest.
  • Further monitoring of specific parameters.
  • Seeking medical assessment when necessary.

These recommendations are intended to support understanding and further evaluation, not replace professional medical advice.

Step 9 — Download PDF

The astronaut can select:

Download PDF

This exports the available Health Intelligence Report for subsequent review.

The report brings together findings, visualizations, biological explanations, and supporting information.

4. What Happens When a Biomarker Is Not Registered?

Medical examination files may contain biomarkers that are not included in the console's existing catalogue.

Instead of automatically treating these parameters as scientifically accepted, THE MITOCHONDRIA provides a structured review process.

The following procedure describes our tested synthetic demonstration workflow.

Stage 1 — Astronaut Submits Five Unknown Biomarkers

For this demonstration, the astronaut uploads an examination containing five previously unregistered biomarkers.

The sequence is:

  1. Sign in as Astronaut.
  2. Open Unified Data Intake.
  3. Select MITOCHONDRIA 2026 – Synthetic Demonstration — Alex Morgan — Synthetic Astronaut.
  4. Select the appropriate synthetic Data Provenance.
  5. Upload the examination containing five unknown biomarkers.
  6. Select Review All Five.
  7. Locate Register Current Batch as a Pending Review Request.
  8. Select Review Metadata Submission.
  9. Review the submission information.
  10. Select I Consent.
  11. Press Submit.

The five items are registered as a pending review request.

The workflow displays their status as Under Review.

Stage 2 — Researcher Reviews the Submitted Biomarkers

Next, an authorized researcher signs into the console.

The sequence is:

  1. Sign out of the Astronaut account.
  2. Select Researcher → Sign In.
  3. Navigate to Jump to Bulk Synthetic.
  4. Open All Requests.
  5. Locate the request containing the five submitted biomarkers.
  6. Select an individual biomarker.
  7. Assign the appropriate scientific domain: Bone, Cardiovascular, Immune, or Behavioral.
  8. Review the submitted information.
  9. Select Accept Selected when appropriate.
  10. Check the result confirmation.

During our demonstration, processing one item generated a confirmation such as Success 1, while four items remained awaiting evaluation.

This illustrates how researchers can process proposed biomarkers individually.

The researcher workspace also supports scientific evidence review and interpretation workflows.

Stage 3 — Ground Medical Reviews and Activates the Item

Following the researcher stage, the relevant synthetic demonstration item can proceed to the Ground Medical activation workflow.

The sequence is:

  1. Sign out of the Researcher account.
  2. Select Medical → Sign In.
  3. Choose the relevant mission.
  4. Select Refresh Pending Reviews, if required.
  5. Open Workflow Status.
  6. Select All Records.
  7. Locate the item processed by the researcher.
  8. Select Activate.
  9. Select Confirm.

The console confirms the activation within the synthetic demonstration workflow.

The resulting catalogue entry can then be available for subsequent supported recognition and processing.

Important scientific distinction: Researcher review, Ground Medical review, and synthetic demonstration activation are not interchangeable with formal scientific or clinical validation.

Our prototype explicitly separates demo approval and activation from scientific evidence assessment. Demonstration activation should never be interpreted as proof that a biomarker has been clinically validated.

This workflow illustrates how a scientific catalogue can expand through structured, human-supervised processes rather than uncontrolled automated acceptance.

5. Live Monitoring — Physiological and Environmental Measurements

Another important direction of THE MITOCHONDRIA is the integration of compatible monitoring devices.

Medical examinations provide information collected at specific points in time. However, astronauts may also benefit from monitoring selected physiological and environmental measurements as conditions change.

Our console includes a Live Monitoring interface designed around this need.

Step 1 — Access Live Monitoring

The astronaut opens the Live Monitoring section of the web console.

Step 2 — Use a Compatible Monitoring Device

The intended device connection uses supported Bluetooth-enabled measurement equipment.

Compatibility requires more than the presence of Bluetooth. The device must expose measurement data through a compatible interface or protocol.

Step 3 — Receive Supported Measurements

Depending on the available equipment, the intended measurements include:

  • Heart Rate: Cardiovascular monitoring.
  • Body Temperature: Physiological temperature monitoring.
  • Environmental Oxygen: Oxygen concentration in the surrounding environment.
  • Environmental Carbon Dioxide: Carbon dioxide concentration in the surrounding environment.
  • Additional Measurements: Other parameters supported by compatible equipment and the console's data interface.

Step 4 — View the Monitoring Information

The monitoring interface is intended to display incoming measurements so that astronauts can review changing values.

This complements the information collected through periodic medical examinations.

Step 5 — Support Integrated Health Monitoring

The broader objective is to combine examination-based information with supported device observations, helping provide a more continuous picture of astronaut health and the surrounding environment.

Current development status: Live device integration and broader Bluetooth compatibility require additional real-device testing. Continuous real-time streaming across arbitrary Bluetooth devices has not been established as a validated capability of the current prototype.

We therefore distinguish the monitoring architecture and demonstrated interface from future device-validation objectives.

6. Technology, Software Architecture, and Data Security

THE MITOCHONDRIA combines scientific research, structured data management, secure mission records, and AI-assisted workflows.

Biological Knowledge

The scientific catalogue contains 70 structured metrics, organized across four health domains.

The project also includes scientific reference handbooks containing:

  • 63 bone reference variables.
  • 96 cardiovascular reference metrics.
  • 117 immune research entries.
  • 99 behavioral research entries.

These handbook entries are research references. They should not be interpreted as an equivalent number of activated biomarkers or clinically validated measurements.

Scientific Reasoning and AI

The system combines structured scientific information with interpretation workflows.

Artificial intelligence may assist with document processing, research questions, and explanatory content.

However, AI-generated scientific content is not automatically considered scientifically approved.

Human research review remains an important part of the project's design.

Secure Mission Records

The architecture includes:

  • Encrypted, offline-first local records.
  • Authorized server-backed access.
  • Role-based permissions.
  • Mission-oriented record organization.
  • Scientific evidence tracking.
  • Researcher and Ground Medical workspaces.

The offline-first approach is particularly relevant to long-duration space missions, where communication with Earth may be delayed or interrupted.

Database and Open Source

The project uses Supabase as part of its database infrastructure.

THE MITOCHONDRIA is an open-source research prototype distributed under the Apache 2.0 licence.

Its implementation and technical documentation are available through the public repository.

GitHub:
https://github.com/computech-gr/MITOCHONDRIA-NASA-Space-Apps-2026

Web Console:
https://mitochondria.edocinfo.com/

7. Creativity and Innovation

The central innovation of THE MITOCHONDRIA is its effort to connect health measurements from multiple physiological systems within a unified scientific environment.

Our approach brings together several elements:

Integrated Biological Reasoning: The console organizes measurements around scientifically relevant relationships rather than presenting only isolated laboratory results.

AI-Assisted Analysis: Artificial intelligence supports selected workflows without replacing scientific or medical judgment.

Three Health-Related User Roles: Astronauts, researchers, and Ground Medical personnel interact with health information according to their responsibilities.

Scientific Review Workflows: Proposed new biomarkers can undergo structured review rather than being automatically accepted.

Longitudinal Health Reports: Examination results from different dates can be examined together.

Monitoring Device Integration: The console is designed to support compatible physiological and environmental monitoring equipment.

Offline-First Architecture: Encrypted local records support workflows in environments where connectivity cannot be guaranteed.

These capabilities reflect our attempt to address the practical challenges of health monitoring beyond Earth.

8. Benefits and Intended Impact

Spaceflight affects multiple physiological systems simultaneously.

NASA's Human Research Program identifies five major hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity fields, and hostile or closed environments.

These hazards can contribute to changes in cardiovascular function, bone and muscle health, immune regulation, sleep, and psychological well-being.

THE MITOCHONDRIA addresses the challenge of understanding these interconnected observations by providing a unified environment for health data organization and scientific interpretation.

Our intended benefits include:

  • Making complex health data easier to understand.
  • Supporting the identification of potentially concerning findings.
  • Improving visibility of changes across examination dates.
  • Supporting structured scientific interpretation.
  • Helping astronauts and authorized personnel review health information.
  • Supporting research into relationships between physiological systems.
  • Providing a foundation for future health monitoring technologies.

During development, our team considered scientific reliability, usability, data privacy, limited connectivity, human oversight, and the needs of long-duration missions.

Current Limitations

THE MITOCHONDRIA is a research prototype demonstrated using synthetic data.

It has not undergone independent clinical validation, is not deployed by NASA, and is not a medical diagnostic device.

Cross-domain biological relationships require further investigation and should not be interpreted as clinically proven causal connections.

Some newer reporting workflows have been verified in the development Preview environment but are not yet confirmed as published on the public website.

Future Development

Our next objectives include:

  • Independent clinical and scientific validation.
  • Testing in astronaut-analogue mission environments.
  • Expanded real-device compatibility testing.
  • Additional validation of cross-domain biological relationships.
  • Improved server-side persistence of interpretation approvals.
  • Continued development of integrated health reporting.

Beyond space exploration, similar approaches could eventually support healthcare in isolated or resource-limited environments on Earth.
